implementation_notes: System.Threading.Channels is the modern .NET realization: Channel.CreateBounded<T>(new BoundedChannelOptions(capacity)) is the bounded buffer, Writer.WriteAsync awaits while the channel is full (backpressure), and Reader.ReadAllAsync (or ReadAsync) drains it with await foreach; Complete() on the writer ends the stream so ReadAllAsync terminates after the last item. The full-mode policy is explicit (BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait/DropOldest/DropNewest/DropWrite) and the channel is safe for multiple producers and consumers without external locking. Choose it whenever the surrounding code is async; BlockingCollection<T> is the older synchronous counterpart.
pitfalls: Forgetting Writer.Complete() leaves await foreach waiting forever after the last item.
DropOldest/DropNewest/DropWrite silently discard items - a deliberate shedding policy that must be chosen consciously, not debugged later as lost work.
Blocking synchronously on WriteAsync (.GetAwaiter().GetResult()) can deadlock in a UI/synchronization context; stay async end to end.
A single Channel<T> hands items out to readers individually, so per-key ordering requires partitioning into several channels.

variants.name: BlockingCollection<T> over a concurrent collection
variants.implementation_notes: BlockingCollection<T> is the classic BCL form: constructed over an IProducerConsumerCollection<T> (typically ConcurrentQueue<T>) with a boundedCapacity, Add blocks while full and Take blocks while empty, TryAdd/TryTake with timeouts give bounded waits, and CompleteAdding marks the end so consumers finish through GetConsumingEnumerable(). It implements IDisposable for cleanup and predates Channels by a decade; it is the right choice on .NET Framework or in strictly synchronous code that cannot adopt async streams, but its blocking API consumes a thread per consumer.
variants.code_sketch:
using var jobs = new BlockingCollection<Job>(boundedCapacity: 1000);

jobs.Add(job);                        // blocks while full
jobs.CompleteAdding();                // end of stream

foreach (var job in jobs.GetConsumingEnumerable())
    Handle(job);                      // blocks while empty
pitfalls: Take() after CompleteAdding() throws InvalidOperationException; guard with IsCompleted or use GetConsumingEnumerable().
Disposing while another thread is blocked in Take is racy - quiesce the producers first.
One blocked thread per consumer: with many slow consumers, prefer Channels and async consumers.
